mcqs.question: Why does RoboDog implementing both Dog and RoboAnimal (each with a conflicting default speak()) require an explicit override?
options: Because interfaces are not allowed to have default methods in Java at all
Because RoboDog must be declared abstract whenever it implements two interfaces
Because default methods can only ever be called through Dog.super, never directly
Because Java refuses to silently pick one interface's default when two conflict, forcing the implementing class to disambiguate
mcqs.explanation: Java 8+ interfaces can have default methods, and when two conflict, the compiler errors rather than guessing — the implementing class must override and pick explicitly. RoboDog doesn't need to be abstract, and default methods can be called normally when there's no conflict.

mcqs.question: Why did Java ban multiple class inheritance but still allow implementing multiple interfaces?
options: Interfaces are always faster to resolve at runtime than classes

The dangerous part of the diamond is conflicting state and implementation from parent classes; interfaces, even with default methods, still can't hold instance fields, so they can't create a state conflict
Multiple interfaces were banned too, until Java 8 introduced default methods
Classes can only have one method each, while interfaces can have many
mcqs.explanation: Fields are the crux — two parent classes can each bring conflicting state, but interfaces (with or without default methods) never hold instance fields, so implementing several never causes a state ambiguity. There's no runtime speed distinction, and multiple interface implementation was always allowed.

mcqs.question: In Python, if `class RoboDog(Dog, RoboAnimal)` doesn't override speak(), and both parents define it, what happens?
options: A runtime error, since Python doesn't allow multiple inheritance
It fails to compile, exactly like Java's default-method conflict
Python's MRO deterministically resolves it — here, to Dog's version, since Dog is listed first — with no error at all
Python always calls both versions and merges their return values
mcqs.explanation: Python computes a deterministic Method Resolution Order via C3 linearization and silently picks accordingly — no error, no merging. Python does allow multiple inheritance, and it isn't compiled ahead-of-time the way Java is, so there's no compile error to raise.

mcqs.question: Why is "the diamond problem is solved by the language silently picking whichever parent it finds first" a wrong general answer?
options: It's only true for Python's MRO — Java's compiler refuses to guess and forces an explicit override, and C++ needs explicit resolution for method conflicts too
No language actually resolves the diamond problem this way, including Python
It's true for every language mentioned, so there's nothing wrong with the statement
The diamond problem only applies to interfaces, never to classes, so the statement is irrelevant
mcqs.explanation: Silently picking the first match describes Python specifically, not a universal fix — Java errors and demands an explicit override, and C++'s virtual inheritance fixes state duplication while method conflicts still need explicit resolution. The diamond applies to both classes (C++) and interfaces (Java).
